meta: Dramas like Lost (2021): the My Mister pairing, and the other Korean dramas about failing quietly.
standfirst: The obvious pairing is My Mister, and it holds completely: two people failing at life, told at the pace of actually failing at life, shot beautifully and plotted barely. Jeon Do Yeon and Ryu Jun Yeol play exhaustion as something physical rather than decorative. The first three episodes are deliberately bleak and episode four is where the two of them finally talk, which is the point to judge it from. It went almost unnoticed because of where it aired and because it is austere enough to read as art-house. Hopeful in the narrowest sense: nothing gets fixed, and staying alive is the achievement.

picks.why: The pairing, and it is not a stretch. Same subject of somebody in their forties who has quietly concluded they are nothing, met by somebody younger with no options left, and the same refusal to make that romantic. Difference: it has an actual plot, an office conspiracy and a neighbourhood full of people, so it fills its hours where this one sits in them.

Two survivors, avoidant and in pain, long before they are in love. Same patience with people who behave badly because they are exhausted, same interest in physical damage that does not photograph well. Difference: it is a proper romance with a conspiracy running underneath, and it commits to recovery, so the last third is warm.

Stasis as the subject, and a family that mostly does not speak. Same pace 1 stillness, same conviction that a small life deserves a full series, same suspicion of anything resembling an event. Difference: it is rural and dryly funny, and liberation is a stated goal rather than something nobody dares name.

Exhausted adults, glacial by design, and honest about grief. Same low light, same long silences, same central pair who are drawn together by shared depletion rather than attraction. Difference: a revenge plan gives it a spine and a direction, so there is always somewhere for a scene to go.

Adults making one real decision slowly. Same naturalism, same pace 1, same respect for the ordinary weight of a family's disapproval. Difference: it is a romance in the daylight, much gentler, and nothing in it is as far gone as either lead here.

Time as the thing that has already been lost. Same subject of a life that did not happen and the same willingness to let a character be bitter about it. Difference: heavy 5, and a structural reveal in the final stretch changes what the whole show was, which this one would never do.

against.title: It's Okay to Not Be Okay
against.why: The healing recommendation everybody reaches for, and it is stylised where this is plain. Fairy-tale framing, a glossy romance and a redemption arc on schedule. Lost is austere and does not believe in rescue, and going from one to the other is a genre change disguised as a follow-up.

against.title: When the Weather Is Fine
against.why: Paired for the quiet, and it is soft rather than bleak. A bookshop, snow, a small town and a romance that heals by proximity. The specific thing Lost does, sitting with somebody who has run out of reasons, is not on offer.

against.title: Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha
against.why: The comfort default, and after this it will read as a lie. Comfort 5, guaranteed soft landing, a village designed to absorb any problem within an episode. Nothing wrong with it; it is just the opposite of what this show is honest about.
